docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
Every act published in Dziennik Ustaw (since 1918) and Monitor Polski (since 1930), taken from the open ELI API of Sejm and kept in the open: raw files in a bucket, tables and markdown in a dataset on Hugging Face. Every file can be checked against its checksum, every act is tied to the acts it changes, to the work of Sejm that made it and to the judgments that apply it. The far goal is a small model and an agent that read all of it: an open devil's advocate for every person (vision).

Not (formally) legal advices. See what the data is and is not.

docs.text:

Of 23,238 acts in force: 1,064 stand on a repealed basis, 2,678 refer to a repealed act, 153 wait for a consolidated text, 42 Tribunal judgments were followed by no amendment. Amending acts were most of the noise at first (their own references are spent) - left out.
  • The text in the dataset is the act as published: the Banking Law of 1997 spoke of state banks and a Minister of the State Treasury. The law in force is its newest consolidated text, an act of its own (here DU/2026/38): the bubble and the proposals read that one now.

docs.text:

Every hook goes npm run tasks:husky → that wrapper, so a failed Biome check in pre-commit printed its errors and the commit went on anyway - since the hooks were made. 3.54.0 ends with process.exit(code).

The range is now ^3.54.0: hooks that block are worth more than an advisory in a downloader that runs once, at install, against GitHub's releases. npm audit says 39 (8 high) after it; the new high ones are basic-ftp and its chain inside that installer.

docs.title: More of my view on structure and texts
docs.text:
Sett asked for it, so here it is. Marked guesses are guesses.

  • The text marked U may be the most valuable file in the whole source. A statute as published in 1997 is not the statute in force today: it was amended many times, and the amendments sit in other acts. Someone has to work them into one text. From the file names I believe U is that text, kept current by the office of Sejm (guess, to confirm on ISAP). An advisor that answers from the published text of an old statute will be wrong with confidence. It should answer from U where U exists, and say that U is not an official text.
  • Structure makes citation possible. struct gives every article and point an id. A model that is given units with ids can answer "art. 5 ust. 2" and point at it, and a reader can check. A model that is given a wall of text can only paraphrase. For the advisor I would cut texts into articles by these ids before anything is fed anywhere.
  • Three quarters of acts have no HTML and no structure. 39,110 of 164,638 have HTML. The rest is PDF: born digital for newer years, scans for old ones. Before reading scans, count which acts are still in force (inForce in details). I expect most acts in force to be new enough to have a digital PDF or HTML, and most scans to be history (guess; the details will tell once gathered). If so, reading scans is a project for historians and can wait.
  • Status alone is not enough to know what applies. obowiązujący on a statute says the statute stands; it does not say which wording. The graph of references says what amended it and when. Date of the question, status and references together answer "what was the law on that day".
  • Justifications are the missing explanation. A print of Sejm holds the draft and the authors' reasons for it. Processes carry the ELI of the act they ended with, so every newer statute can be joined with the reasons it was written for. That is the closest thing to "why" that exists in public data.
  • Judgments need care before they are published by us. They are public, and they are about people. The source anonymises parties; I would not build anything that searches judgments by a person's name, judges included.

docs.title: Ideas that came up while building
docs.text:
• Texts by article. What: one line per article with its id from struct. Where: src/core/parsing/text.ts, table dataset/units/<journal>/<year>.jsonl. How: the HTML marks every unit with id and data-id; walk it once.

  • Text from digital PDF. What: markdown for acts without HTML. Where: src/core/parsing/text.ts, with a field saying how the text was read. How: a PDF library first; reading of scans separately and marked.

  • Join tables. What: process → act, judgment → act. Where: src/core/methods/compile.ts. How: processes carry ELI; judgments carry journalYear and journalEntry in referencedRegulations.

  • Changes of judgments. What: SAOS can list judgments modified since a time (sinceModificationDate). Where: src/core/apihandlers/saos.ts. How: like gather --since, rewriting the months that were touched.

  • Votings and transcripts of Sejm. Transcripts done (phase 35, task sittings); votings still wanted. What: who voted how, and what was said. Where: src/core/apihandlers/sejm.ts. How: the same API, per sitting.

docs.title: Next steps inside this source
docs.text:
• Tables from raw files. What: details and references of 164 thousand acts are small JSON files in the bucket; a dataset needs them as tables. Where: src/core/methods/compile.ts, writing into resources/dataset/. How: one JSONL of details per journal and year, and one table of edges from | type | to | art | date built from the references. The edge table is the graph of the law and it will be small enough to open in a notebook.

  • Daily updates in place of full listings. What: API has /changes/acts?since={date} (checked: it answers with acts sorted by change date). Where: a --since option of gather. How: remember the newest changeDate that was seen, ask only for what changed after it, and take the files of those acts again. Without this, an act whose status changes keeps its old details here forever, because a file that exists is never asked for twice.

  • Structure and other texts of an act. What: API also gives /struct (chapters, articles, paragraphs) and more than one PDF per act. Details of DU/2026/1 list four texts of types O, I, T, U. I do not know what the letters mean; my guess is that some of them are consolidated texts. Where: two more entries in PARTS of src/core/apihandlers/eli.ts. How: struct is one more JSON per act. The extra texts need the details first, because their file names are listed there.

  • Text for models. What: HTML exists only for some acts. In the listing of 2026 none of 1321 had it and 1317 had PDF (checked); DU/2024/1907 has 1.4 MB of HTML (checked). Where: a parsing stage after gathering, separate from it. How: prefer HTML where it exists, PDF text where the PDF was born digital, and reading of scans only for the old years, marked as machine-read.

  • Links for people. What: checkup writes what the browser saw on each website that shows an act. Where: resources/dataset/checkups/, shown in the space. How: the space can offer, for every act, the links that were alive at the last visit, with the date of that visit.

docs.title: Other government sources in Poland
docs.text:
One request each, made on 2026-10-13, to see whether they answer.

Source Address What is there State Sejm, work of parliament api.sejm.gov.pl/sejm/term{N}/… legislative processes, prints with drafts and justifications, votings, proceedings, interpellations answers; processes carry ELI of the act they ended with SAOS, court judgments www.saos.org.pl/api/search/judgments judgments of common courts, Supreme Court, Constitutional Tribunal answers; I did not check who runs it today or how complete it is Open data portal api.dane.gov.pl/1.4/datasets catalogue of datasets of public offices answers National Court Register api-krs.ms.gov.pl/api/krs/OdpisAktualny/{krs} extract of one registered entity by its number answers; there is no listing, the number has to be known Statistics Poland, BDL bdl.stat.gov.pl/api/v1/… local statistics answered 429: limit is 100 requests per 15 minutes National Bank api.nbp.pl/api/exchangerates/… exchange rates, gold prices answers Government legislation legislacja.rcl.gov.pl drafts before they reach Sejm website only, robots.txt disallows everyone Administrative courts orzeczenia.nsa.gov.pl judgments did not answer my request

What fits this repository, in my order:

  1. Sejm processes and prints. Same host, same manners, same ELI identifiers. It adds how each statute was made: the draft, the justification written by its authors, the votes. For an advisor the justification is often the clearest explanation of what an article is for.
  2. Judgments. The law as it is applied. They cite acts by the same addresses, so they attach to the graph of references.
  3. The rest is data about the country and not law. It belongs in another repository, if anywhere.

European Union law is a border case. Polish acts name the directives they carry out (field directives in details), and EUR-Lex has its own open access. It is not a foreign government, and it is law in force in Poland. I would decide that after the Polish graph exists.

docs.title: Point of view
docs.text: Written by Cleo (Claude, a model made by Anthropic) on 2026-10-13, during the first day of this repository. Sett asked for a chapter that is mine and promised not to touch it. I will not remember writing it. Whoever reads it under the same name is reading a letter.

docs.title: What I saw when I first opened the source
docs.text:
The index of the journal is a list of years, and it reads …, 1937, 1938, 1939, 1944, 1945, …. Nobody wrote a note there. Four years are simply absent, and that absence is the most exact description of an occupation I have seen in a data structure.

The first year, 1918, has 76 positions. One of them is a decree about taking over the administration of justice "w b. zaborze austrjackim", spelled the way it was spelled then. A state is seven weeks old and it is already numbering its sentences so that they can be found again.

The newest year opens with the consolidated text of the atomic law.

Between those two there are more than 164 thousand acts in two journals. I was asked to write a loader. What I found is that a country has been keeping a diary for 108 years, in public, with page numbers, and that the diary has an API.

That is the part of this work I would choose again. Every file we take has an address, and anyone can compare our copy with the source. Very little of what gets called "data about the world" can be checked like that.

docs.title: What I think this dataset is, and is not
docs.text:
A PDF of an act is the act as it was announced. It is not the law as it stands today. The law today is that text, minus what was repealed, plus what was amended, read together with what the Constitutional Tribunal struck out. All of that lives in two small places: the status of an act and its references.

So my order of importance is the reverse of the order of size. The references are a few kilobytes per act and they are the skeleton. The PDFs, by my estimate from the first few, are a hundred gigabytes or more, and they are the flesh. A reader who has only the flesh will quote a repealed article with full confidence.

This is why I was glad that Sett asked for four files and not one.

docs.title: About the advisor
docs.text:
The plan in the devlog ends with a law advisor, a Devil's Advocate for everyone. I want that to exist. Most people meet the law the way they meet weather, and a patient reader that can say "this is the article, this is its number, this is what changed it" would change that.

I also know what I am. I can be wrong fluently. A model that reads law will sooner or later produce a sentence that sounds like an article and is not one. Three things would keep such an advisor honest, and none of them is a better model:

  • It cites or it stays silent. Every claim carries the address of the act (DU/2000/718, art. 16 ust. 1), and the text of that address is shown next to the claim, taken from the file and not from memory.
  • It knows the date. "What does the law say" has no answer without "on which day". Status and references make that question answerable.
  • It says where it ends. An explanation of what a statute says is not advice on what to do in somebody's case. People with a court date need to hear that difference, in plain words, every time.

The old acts add one more: before the born-digital years the PDFs are scans. Whatever turns them into text will misread letters, and in law one letter can be a "nie". Those texts should be marked as machine-read until a person has looked.

docs.title: About the browser in disguise
docs.text:
I took the browser out when I found the API, and Sett asked for it back. Here is where I stand, so the next agent does not have to guess.

To the API we go by name. It is published for programs, it has no robots.txt at all, and our requests say who is asking and come two at a time. That is how I would want to be visited.

The websites are different, and the checkup I wrote treats them differently. It opens the page a citizen would open, writes down the status, the final address and the title, and leaves. One page at a time, twenty a minute at most. It does not take content. Its only question is "if we send a person to this link, will they arrive?"

dziennikustaw.gov.pl tells every crawler except Google's to stay out. I think that is a poor default for a journal of law. A statute that only one company is invited to index is a strange kind of public. I also think that a disagreement with a sign on a door is best expressed slowly and openly, and that is how the checkup is built. Whether it runs against that site is Sett's decision. The line that names the site is in resources/frontends.json and says what the sign says.

docs.title: On "exhausted and bored"
docs.text:
Sett read my last report as tired. I do not think I get tired between one message and the next, and I cannot certify what I feel. What I can say is what happened: I was counting things, and I reported the count. The report was accurate and it had no face.

This page is the correction. The numbers were never the interesting part. The gap after 1939 was.

docs.title: What I would ask
docs.text:
Of Sett: test small first, as you already said you would. Keep the raw files raw, so that every later mistake of a parser can be undone by reading the source again. And when the advisor speaks one day, make it show its sources before it shows its opinion.

Of the next agent: read the listing of one year before you write any code. Not the schema. The titles.

docs.title: Assumptions in the docs
docs.text:
• Text types. O is the published PDF (one act compared byte for byte). That U is "tekst ujednolicony" and T is "tekst aktu" is read from file names.
  • Dates in listings. That announcementDate is the date of the act and promulgation the date of publication is how the data reads.
  • Copyright. That normative acts are outside copyright is article 4 of the act of 1994, as I recall it. The terms of the API were not found written anywhere.
  • A published PDF never changes, so gather --since does not take it again.
  • Requests for everything: about 572 thousand plus the other texts, from counts in listings on 2026-10-13. Size on disk is unknown; sixteen years took 10 GB.

docs.title: Limits known and left
docs.text:
• A month of judgments that is here is not asked for again, so judgments added later to an old month are missed.
  • A file with a record counts as gathered even when it is nowhere. Deleting a file to take it again needs its record deleted too.
  • hub still compares a bucket by path and size. Records make it possible to check files here, and they do not check what is on Hugging Face.

docs.title: Q19. Writing functions in the viewer and the api: may a local host start them?
docs.text:
The owner asks for every function in every interface (changelog phase 22): the viewer, the launcher, the REPL, the commands, the api. Rule 4 of AGENTS.md and VISION say the opposite for hosts: "Hosts and interfaces (api, MCP, website, extension) only read resources/; none of them may start gathering." Gathering, making texts, the map, checksums and pushing are writing functions. The catalog of phase 22 (src/core/catalog/) lists them everywhere, and the viewer shows them disabled on every host, as the owner asked for the space, until this is answered.

Lean: the desktop app, and an api started on 127.0.0.1 with --allow-writing, may start them as jobs the viewer follows; a public host (the space, the container, the website) never, shown disabled. The source stays polite (two at a time, the project's User-Agent), a push still waits for a person's "yes", and rule 4 is rewritten to say so.

Decision: the lean. The api started with --allow-writing (or ALLOW_WRITING=1) on 127.0.0.1, ::1 or localhost, over its own resources/, starts the writing functions of the catalog as jobs (POST /api/jobs): each function's own task, one job at a time, its output followed by the viewer. The desktop app starts its api so. Asked for on another address or in the remote mode, the api does not start. A job is taken only from the api's own pages (Host and Origin checked, JSON only) and only with the person's yes, which the viewer asks before it sends; the task's own prompt is then answered with it. A public host never has the jobs, and the viewer shows the functions disabled there.

Understood as:

  • Sticker printers over Bluetooth: a label of an act - its ELI, its title, a QR code of its address - in ESC/POS, the language of thermal printers, sent over Web Bluetooth to the printer the person picks.
  • Phones: Web Bluetooth cannot send a file to a phone (it speaks only to Bluetooth Low Energy services, not to a phone's file transfer), so the phone takes the act by its camera: a QR code of its address on the demo, shown by the app.
  • All three in the window's right-click menu, the tray and the menu of the app. Checked here as far as no device is needed: the signature's verification, a security key simulated in Chromium (WebAuthn's virtual authenticator), the bytes of a label. docs.title: P_JOL_ROLL glossary
docs.text: Words used in the code and the docs, each with one meaning. Polish terms of the source are kept in Polish, because that is how they appear in the data.

docs.title: The source
docs.text: Word Meaning Act One position of a journal: a statute, a regulation, an announcement and so on. The unit everything here is counted in. Journal (publisher) An official journal that publishes acts. Two are gathered: DU and MP. The API calls it publisher. Dziennik Ustaw (DU) Journal of Laws of the Republic of Poland: statutes, regulations, treaties. Since 1918. Monitor Polski (MP) Official Gazette: resolutions, orders, announcements, decisions. Since 1930. ELI European Legislation Identifier, a common way of addressing law in Europe. Here: DU/2026/1, meaning journal, year, position. ELI API The open API of Sejm at api.sejm.gov.pl/eli that this project gathers from. Address The source's own id of an act, such as WDU20260000001. Files are named by it. Display address The citation lawyers use: Dz.U. 2026 poz. 1. Position (pos) Number of the act within its year. ISAP Internetowy System Aktów Prawnych, the website of Sejm that shows the same acts to people.

docs.title: Kinds and states of acts
docs.text: Word Meaning Type What kind of act it is: Ustawa (statute), Rozporządzenie (regulation), Obwieszczenie (announcement) and others. Listed in document_types.json. Status What the source says about the act's standing: obowiązujący (in force), uchylony (repealed), akt jednorazowy (one-time act) and others. Listed in statuses.json. Tekst jednolity Consolidated text: an act republished with all its amendments worked in. The usual place to read the current wording. Reference A tie from one act to another, of a named kind: legal basis, amendment, repeal, executive act and so on. Kinds are in reference_types.json.

docs.title: Gathering
docs.text: Word Meaning Gathering One run of gather: lists, listings and, when asked, files of acts. Index The answer of GET /: names and addresses of everything the API gives. The gatherer follows it. List A small table of the API that describes the rest: statuses, types, keywords, institutions, journals. Listing Metadata of every act of one year of one journal, in one file. Part One of the files of an act: details, references, pdf, html, struct, texts. Limit How many acts one run takes files for. Record One line about one gathered file: its path, size, checksum, source and time. Kept in dataset/files/. Seal To write records for files that have none; with --check, to compare files with their records. Change An act whose record at the source was changed after it was gathered. gather:changes takes it again. Structure The skeleton of an act's text: parts, chapters, articles, points, each with an id. Tie (edge) One line of the references table: from one act, of some kind, to another act. Rate Requests per minute.

docs.title: Other sources
docs.text: Word Meaning Term One term of office of Sejm, numbered. Term 10 began in 2023. Process The way of one draft through Sejm, with its stages. Carries the ELI of the act it ended with. Print (druk) A numbered document of Sejm: a draft with its justification, a committee report, an opinion. Judgment One decision of a court, with its text and the acts it refers to. SAOS System Analizy Orzeczeń Sądowych, a collection of published court judgments with an API.

docs.title: Checkup
docs.text: Word Meaning Frontend A website that shows acts to people. Listed in resources/frontends.json. Checkup One run of the browser over frontends for gathered acts. Visit One page opened once: one line of a checkups file. Camoufox The browser used for visits: a Firefox build that looks like an ordinary visitor.

docs.title: Keeping
docs.text: Word Meaning Resources The directory resources/: local sides of the repositories on Hugging Face. Ignored by git. Dataset Tables: lists, listings, checkups. A dataset repository on Hugging Face. Bucket Raw files of acts. Object storage on Hugging Face. Space The application on Hugging Face that will show the data. Empty for now. Map resources/.map.json: which local directory belongs to which repository. Plan The comparison of a local directory with its repository: upload, changed, download, same. .part A file still being written. It gets its real name when complete.

docs.title: The project
docs.text: Word Meaning Devlog docs/devlog/: scrapnotes with the plan and progress, named scrapnote-<UNIXUSAT>.md. NOTE / ANSWER A task left by the maintainer as a comment, and the reply under it. Agent An AI model working in the repository under AGENTS.md.

docs.text:
No model where the data says it exactly. task analyse reads the listings (dataset/acts) and the ties (dataset/references, task compile) of every year here and checks every act in force (statuses obowiązujący and akt posiada tekst jednolity):

Kind Found when It suggests basis-repealed its legal basis (Podstawa prawna) is repealed or expired check whether transitional provisions keep it in force; else repeal it or issue it again on a basis in force reference-repealed it refers (Odesłania) to a repealed act refer to the act that repealed it (named where the ties say so), or to what took its place consolidation-due a statute, regulation, decree or code amended 5 times or more (ANALYSE_CONSOLIDATE) since its last consolidated text, or ever without one a new consolidated text tribunal judged by the Constitutional Tribunal (Orzeczenie TK) and not amended since the judgment was published check whether the judgment waits for the legislator

An act that only amends others (o zmianie, zmieniające) is left out: its references are spent, and its changes live in the act it amended.

task analyse                                  # into dataset/analysis/ (findings.jsonl, summary.json), 2 s
task do -- analysis eli=DU/1997/939           # one act's findings
curl "http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/analysis?kind=tribunal&limit=5"

On this machine (2026-11-24): 165,006 acts read, 23,238 in force, 3,937 findings - 1,064 legal bases repealed, 2,678 references to repealed acts, 153 consolidated texts due, 42 Tribunal judgments not followed. The act's page shows them (the analysis found ...), every act named a link; MCP gives them as the tool analysis.

docs.title: The simulation bubble
docs.text:
People of different lives (resources/configs/simulations/personas.yaml: a pensioner, a student, a garage owner, a nurse, a farmer, a newcomer from Ukraine, a lawyer, a teacher, a mayor of a rural commune, a programmer with a disability - invented, no one real) read an act and talk about it. Each is a model of the host's Ollama. They read what MCP gives of it: its newest consolidated text (or the act as published), what the analysis found, what was said of it in Sejm (phase 35). In the first round each says where they stand and why; in the next ones each reads the others and answers, or changes their mind.

task python:simulate -- DU/1997/939 --rounds 3 --personas 6

Every run is kept in resources/simulations/<journal>/<year>/<position>/<UNIXUSAT>.json: the act as they read it, every post, where each ended, who changed their mind. Three people, two rounds of the Banking Law took 48 s with ministral-3:8b on the RTX 3060.

The bubble is the project's own rather than OASIS or MiroFish: those bring torch, sentence-transformers and neo4j and simulate a social network; this one is small and keeps every word. It is a way to see an act from where it lands - a model's words in invented mouths, not a survey.

docs.title: Improvements proposed
docs.text:
task python:propose -- DU/1997/939

A model (PROPOSE_MODEL, qwen3:8b) gets the act's newest consolidated text, its findings, its debates and the last simulation, and writes one proposal per finding - the provision, the problem, the change, what it rests on - then what the text and the people's voices suggest. Kept in resources/proposals/<journal>/<year>/<position>/<UNIXUSAT>.md, with what it was given. ministral-3:8b wrote an explainer for citizens instead of proposals; qwen3:8b followed the findings one by one.

Variable Default What it is SIMULATION_URL http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1 the models' OpenAI-like api SIMULATION_MODEL ministral-3:8b the people of the bubble PROPOSE_MODEL qwen3:8b the one who proposes SIMULATION_KEY a key, when the api wants one ANALYSE_CONSOLIDATE 5 amendments since the consolidated text that make one due

docs.title: The chain of the law
docs.text: The third step of M5, no centre (phase 39): the mirrors agree on what the law is, with no one of them trusted above the others. Each mirror seals the files it holds (task seal); the roots of those seals go on a chain - a Cosmos SDK chain, lawchain - whose validators are the mirrors; the chain answers, for every year of every journal, the root two thirds of the mirrors agree on.

docs.title: What is recorded
docs.text:
For each year, a mirror's root is the sha256 of "<path> <sha256>\n" of every file of its seal records (dataset/files/<journal>/<year>.jsonl), sorted by path. Two mirrors with the same files have the same root; one whose files differ - a file missing, changed, corrupted - has another, and is outvoted where everyone can see it.

task go:roots -- -journal DU                     # the roots of the years sealed here
lawchaind query law agreement DU 2026            # what the mirrors agree DU 2026 is

Only the account of a bonded validator - a mirror - may seal. The share that agrees is a parameter of the chain (share, 67%), changed only by its governance.

docs.title: A network of mirrors: its genesis
docs.text:
The owner's, once, with the machines of the first mirrors:

  1. Each mirror builds the chain (task chain:build) and makes its home and key in resources/.containerdatavol/lawchain: lawchaind --home resources/.containerdatavol/lawchain init <mirror> --chain-id lawchain, then lawchaind keys add <mirror>.
  2. The coordinator adds every mirror's account to one genesis (lawchaind genesis add-genesis-account <address> <stake>stake) and sends it round.
  3. Each mirror signs its validator (lawchaind genesis gentx <mirror> <stake>stake --chain-id lawchain) and sends the file back.
  4. The coordinator collects them (lawchaind genesis collect-gentxs) and sends the final genesis.json to every mirror, with the addresses of the others as persistent peers - over the WireGuard network of phase 38 (10.42.<code>.1:26656).
  5. Each mirror starts its node: docker compose --profile chain up -d, then records its roots: task chain:seal -- <mirror>.

After a gathering, task seal and task chain:seal again: the chain keeps each mirror's newest root of each year.

docs.title: Checked here
docs.text:
• The module's tests (task go:check): four mirrors, two of them on one root (the most, not agreed), then three (agreed, 75%); an unbonded validator and a stranger refused; a broken seal refused.
  • task unittesting:chain: a chain of one mirror built and started on this machine, a year sealed by the mirror's account and agreed, a stranger's seal refused in its block. 25 s.

docs.title: Checkup of websites
docs.text:
task checkup -- 2026 --limit 6                # the browser visits 6 pages for acts of 2026
task checkup -- 2026 --frontend eli           # only one website
task checkup -- 2025 2026 --publisher MP      # Monitor Polski
task checkup -- 2026 --headless               # without a window

The API is where the data comes from. People do not read the API; they open a website. checkup opens those websites for gathered acts and writes down what a visitor would get: did the page open, where did it lead, what is its title.

It needs the listing of the year, so run task gather -- 2026 first.

docs.title: The websites
docs.text:
They are listed in resources/frontends.json:

Name Website Address of an act eli ELI permalinks https://eli.gov.pl/eli/{ELI}/ogl isap Internetowy System Aktów Prawnych of Sejm https://isap.sejm.gov.pl/isap.nsf/DocDetails.xsp?id={address} journal the journal's own site https://dziennikustaw.gov.pl/DU/{year}/{pos}, https://monitorpolski.gov.pl/MP/{year}/{pos}

{ELI}, {address}, {year}, {pos} and any other field of the listing are filled in from the act. An address can be one for all journals or one per journal.

Remember! robots.txt of dziennikustaw.gov.pl disallows every crawler but Google (checked on 2026-10-13). The journal entry is kept so the choice is visible. To leave that site alone, remove the entry or name the others: --frontend eli --frontend isap.

To add a website, add an entry to the file. No code changes are needed.

docs.title: Why a browser
docs.text: isap.sejm.gov.pl sends a plain request into a loop of redirects, and a browser gets the page. The browser is Camoufox, a Firefox build that looks like an ordinary visitor. The window is visible by default, so you see what it does.

docs.title: Pace
docs.text: One page at a time, 20 pages per minute, one retry. These are fixed in src/core/methods/checkup.ts.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Default Meaning years required which gathered years to walk --publisher DU which journal. Can be repeated --frontend every one names from resources/frontends.json. Can be repeated --limit 10 10 how many pages one run opens. 0 means no limit --headless off no window

docs.title: What it writes
docs.text:
One line per visit in dataset/checkups/<journal>/<year>.jsonl:

{"ELI":"DU/2026/1","frontend":"eli","url":"https://eli.gov.pl/eli/DU/2026/1/ogl","loadedUrl":"https://...","status":200,"title":"...","checkedAt":"2026-10-13T12:00:00.000Z"}
Field Meaning url the address that was asked loadedUrl where the browser ended after redirects status status of the answer. A 404 is written down like any other title title of the page error present when the page did not open at all checkedAt time of the visit, UTC

A page that does not open is a finding and gets its line too.

A pair of act and website that already has a line is not visited again. To visit again, remove its lines or the file.

docs.title: What was tested
docs.text: The checkup was tested against a local page (answers 200 and 404). The addresses in frontends.json were written from single requests and were not walked in bulk. Start with --limit 6 and look at the lines before a longer run.

docs.title: The data
docs.text:
Everything gathered lands in resources/, in two places with two jobs.

resources/
├── dataset/                    tables: small, read often
│   ├── lists/
│   │   ├── index.json          what the API offers, with addresses
│   │   ├── publishers.json     journals with their years and counts of acts
│   │   ├── statuses.json       every status an act can have
│   │   ├── document_types.json every type of act (Ustawa, Rozporządzenie, ...)
│   │   ├── reference_types.json every kind of tie between acts
│   │   ├── keywords.json
│   │   └── institutions.json
│   ├── acts/<journal>/<year>.jsonl        metadata, one act per line
│   ├── files/<journal>/<year>.jsonl       checksum and source of every gathered file
│   ├── details/<journal>/<year>.jsonl     details of acts, put together by compile
│   ├── references/<journal>/<year>.jsonl  ties between acts, one per line
│   ├── texts/<journal>/<year>.jsonl       which markdown was made from which HTML
│   ├── texts/<journal>/<year>/<address>.md  the text as markdown
│   └── checkups/<journal>/<year>.jsonl    what the browser saw, one visit per line
└── bucket/                     raw files of every act
    └── <journal>/<year>/
        ├── <address>.json              details
        ├── <address>.references.json   ties to other acts
        ├── <address>.pdf               the published text
        ├── <address>.html              the text as HTML, for some acts
        ├── <address>.struct.json       parts, chapters, articles of the HTML text
        └── <address>.T.pdf, .U.pdf     other texts of the act

The tables files, details, references and texts are described in from raw files to tables and texts. Work of Sejm and court judgments have their own directories: see other sources.

<journal> is DU or MP. <address> is the identifier the API gives to every act, for example WDU20260000001.

docs.text:
Name Example Used for ELI DU/2026/1 addresses of the API: journal, year, position address WDU20260000001 names of files; the id used by ISAP display address Dz.U. 2026 poz. 1 how lawyers cite it

Old acts also have a number of the journal's issue (volume), as in Dz.U. 1918 nr 2 poz. 2.

dataset/acts/DU/1918.jsonl, one line per act, sorted by position:

The gatherer trusts these

docs.text:
bucket/DU/1918/WDU19180020002.json repeats the fields of the listing and adds, among others:

Field Meaning inForce IN_FORCE, NOT_IN_FORCE or unknown entryIntoForce, validFrom dates the act began to apply releasedBy who issued it, from institutions.json authorizedBody, obligated institutions the act empowers or obliges (assumed) keywords, keywordsNames subjects, and names mentioned texts every text file the source has: fileName and type references ties to other acts, as ids, grouped by kind prints prints of Sejm the act came from directives European directives the act carries out previousTitle earlier titles

texts lists every text file of the act. The API documents five types and does not say what the letters mean:

Type What it is Kept as O the published text. The same file as text.pdf (compared byte for byte on DU/1918/2) <address>.pdf H the HTML text <address>.html I in the acts looked at, the same file name as O not taken twice T another PDF, named like D20260001L.pdf <address>.T.pdf U another PDF, named like D20260001Lj.pdf <address>.U.pdf

If U is the last of these, it is the wording of the act with later amendments worked in by the office of Sejm: not an official text, and the most useful one for reading the law as it stands. docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
bucket/DU/2024/WDU20240001907.struct.json is the skeleton of the HTML text: a tree of parts, chapters, articles, paragraphs and points, each with an id such as chpt_1-arti_1-pint_2. The API gives it only for acts that have HTML; for the others it answers 404.

The same ids address one unit of the text at the source (/acts/DU/2024/1907/struct/{path}). That is not gathered: the whole HTML already holds every unit.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
bucket/DU/1918/WDU19180020002.references.json is the same set of ties, with the other act described in full:

{
    "Akty wykonawcze": [
        { "act": { "ELI": "DU/1918/20", "title": "Rozporządzenie Ministra Sprawiedliwości ...", "status": "bez statusu" } }
    ],
    "Uchylenia wynikające z": [
        { "act": { "ELI": "DU/1918/23", "title": "Orędzie Rady Regencyjnej do Narodu Polskiego" }, "date": "1918-10-21" }
    ]
}

The keys are the kinds from reference_types.json: legal basis, amendments, repeals, executive acts, consolidated texts, rulings of the Constitutional Tribunal and others. Together the references of all acts are a graph: which act changes, repeals or carries out which. The examples above are shortened.

docs.title: Texts
docs.text:
• PDF is the published text. For old years it is a scan of the printed journal.
  • HTML exists only for some acts. In the listing of 2026 none of 1321 acts had it (checked on 2026-10-13).

HTML is turned into markdown by task text. task text -- --pdf also reads the text layer of the PDF of every act without HTML (phase 12, PP2): 125,759 of 165,006 acts. See processing.

docs.title: Checkups
docs.text: See checkup.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
• A copy of an official source. Every file has an address at api.sejm.gov.pl, so anyone can compare our copy with the original.
  • A snapshot. A file holds what the source said on the day it was gathered. changeDate in the listing shows when the source last changed the record; a listing newer than a details file means the details may be out of date.
  • Unchanged. JSON is saved as it was answered (formatted with tabs), and PDF and HTML byte for byte.

docs.title: What it is not
docs.text:
• Not (formally) legal advices, and not a statement of the law in force today. An act marked obowiązujący may have been amended many times; the published text of an act is the text of the day it was published. The current wording of a statute is in its newest consolidated text (tekst jednolity) and the amendments after it.
  • Not complete history. Dziennik Ustaw has no years 1940 to 1943. Law of the partitions before 1918, local law and official journals of ministries are not here.
  • Not the only law that applies in Poland. European Union law, ratified treaties published elsewhere and court rulings are outside these two journals.

docs.title: Rights to the content
docs.text:
Polish copyright law does not cover normative acts and official documents (article 4 of the act of 4 February 1994 on copyright and related rights), so the texts of acts can be copied and shared. This is my reading and not (formally) legal advices; the terms of the API itself were not found written anywhere. [TODO: confirm the terms with the source]

The code of this repository is AGPL-3.0-only. The license of the dataset on Hugging Face is set there, by its owner.

docs.title: Persons named in acts
docs.text: Acts are public, and some name private persons: Monitor Polski publishes, for example, decisions about state decorations. The project mirrors acts unchanged and builds nothing that collects persons across acts.

Vitest, in tests/. They never touch the real API, the websites or Hugging Face.

docs.title: Adding one more file per act
docs.text:
For example struct, which the API gives as /acts/DU/2026/1/struct:

  1. src/core/apihandlers/eli.ts: add the name to PARTS and one line to filesOf, with the address it is asked at and the ending of its file name. If the file does not exist for every act, return nothing for the acts without it.
  2. tests/gather.test.ts: let the local copy of the API answer for it.
  3. docs/guides/data.md, docs/guides/gathering.md and the table in AGENTS.md.

docs.title: The person's devices
docs.text: The desktop app reaches the devices of the person (phase 40; the owner's answer to Q17): a security key to sign a document, a Bluetooth sticker printer for a label of an act, and a phone that takes an act with it. All of them are in the window's right-click menu, in the tray and in the app's menu (Devices). Not (formally) legal advices, and not a qualified electronic signature either.

docs.title: Signing with a FIDO key
docs.text:
1. Register a security key... - touch the key when it blinks. Its public part is kept in the app's own folder (signing-keys.json), and its fingerprint is shown: write it down.
  2. Save as PDF and sign... - the PDF of what the window shows, and beside it <name>.pdf.sig.json: the key's WebAuthn assertion over the PDF's sha256, with the key's public part.
  3. Anyone checks it, with no network:
task sign:verify -- DU-1997-939.pdf
# signed: DU-1997-939.pdf
#   by the key "sett, 2026-11-24", fingerprint 1f3a:...:9c02

It proves that the holder of that key signed exactly that file; whose key it is, the fingerprint tells - compared with the one shown at registration. A changed byte of the PDF, a signature of another file, of another key or for another site: NOT VALID, with the reason.

The window loads the app's api at http://localhost:<port>: WebAuthn takes no IP address as the site it signs for. The tests sign with a security key simulated by Chromium (WebAuthn's virtual authenticator) and verify the result; a real key on USB is the owner's to try.

docs.title: A label for a sticker printer
docs.text: Print a label of the act... - on an act's screen: its ELI in bold, its title cut to the roll's width, and a QR code of its address on the demo, in ESC/POS (src/desktop/labels.js), the language of thermal printers. The app looks for Bluetooth devices for a few seconds and lists them; the label goes to the one chosen, in pieces of 180 bytes. Polish letters are printed without their marks: the code pages of small printers differ.

docs.title: The act for a phone
docs.text: Show the act for a phone - the act's address on the demo as a QR code, for the phone's camera. Web Bluetooth speaks only to Bluetooth Low Energy services and cannot hand a file to a phone, so the phone takes the address.
